title: Uttar Pradesh Cracks Down on Fake Paneer and Khoya With Strict New Order
excerpt: UP joins Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh in banning adulterated dairy products as India's anti-fake-paneer movement gains momentum across states.
body:
• Uttar Pradesh has issued a strict anti-adulteration order targeting fake paneer, khoya, and other adulterated milk products across the state.
  • The order follows Maharashtra's one-year ban on analogue paneer issued on July 30, making UP the latest state to join the crackdown.
  • FSSAI has directed all states to launch enforcement drives against adulteration of milk products, with a potential nationwide ban on analogue paneer under review.
  • Testing in Maharashtra found 35% of paneer samples failed quality standards, with restaurants serving analogue paneer as genuine without informing customers.

UP's Sweeping Anti-Adulteration Order

Uttar Pradesh has issued a strict new order banning the manufacture, sale, and distribution of adulterated paneer, khoya, and other fake milk products across the state. The directive targets the sprawling network of dairy adulteration that has long plagued India's most populous state, where festive-season raids routinely turn up thousands of kilograms of synthetic dairy products.

The order empowers food safety officials to conduct surprise raids at milk distribution centres, markets, and retail outlets. Offenders face severe penalties, with the state government previously invoking the stringent National Security Act (NSA) against dairy adulterators — one of the harshest legal tools available for food safety enforcement in India.

UP's Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) has been at the front lines of India's dairy adulteration crisis. In recent enforcement drives, authorities have seized massive quantities of fake dairy products — including synthetic khoya made from vegetable oils and chemicals, and paneer manufactured from palmolein oil, skimmed milk powder, acetic acid, and emulsifiers without a trace of actual milk.

A State-by-State Crackdown Gathers Force

UP's order follows Maharashtra's decision on July 30 to impose a one-year ban on analogue paneer statewide. Maharashtra's Food Safety Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe issued the prohibition after a year-long enforcement drive revealed persistent violations.

The numbers from Maharashtra were damning: of 308 paneer samples collected between April 2025 and March 2026, 109 — a staggering 35.4% — failed to meet prescribed standards. Thirty samples were classified as outright unsafe. Laboratories detected vegetable fats substituted for milk fat, and FDA inspections found restaurants serving analogue paneer as genuine without any disclosure on menus or invoices.

"Serving products in the guise of genuine paneer is now considered an unfair trade practice under the Food Safety and Standards Act."

— Maharashtra FDA

Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh have also moved against analogue dairy products, creating a growing patchwork of state-level bans that is putting pressure on the central government to act decisively.

FSSAI Eyes Nationwide Ban

At the national level, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has been tightening the screws. The regulator's Central Advisory Committee finalized a proposal in October 2025, formally adopted in March 2026, to ban analogue paneer outright and phase out manufacturing licenses for producers of these products.

FSSAI has also directed all states and union territories to launch special enforcement drives against adulteration and misbranding of milk products, including paneer and khoya. The directive mandates intensive inspections, enforcement sampling, licence cancellations, and real-time reporting on the Food Safety Compliance System.

If the proposal reaches its final stage, it could spell the end of a large market for cheap, non-standardized dairy analogues that are high in fat and low in nutritional value. India's ₹65,000-crore paneer market — the world's largest — has been infiltrated by these imitation products, which undercut genuine dairy producers while putting millions of consumers at risk.

Why It Matters for Indian Families

Paneer is one of India's primary protein sources, particularly for the country's large vegetarian population. The health risks from adulterated versions are severe: synthetic paneer made with detergent, urea, or industrial chemicals can cause food poisoning, kidney damage, liver cirrhosis, and long-term organ failure.

For Indian families in the diaspora, the crackdown underscores an ongoing concern about food safety standards when visiting India or purchasing imported Indian dairy products. The state-by-state bans and FSSAI's push for national regulation represent the most coordinated effort yet to protect the integrity of a staple that sits at the center of Indian cuisine.
